What does it mean to belong to an ethnic community or group? And who gets to decide? From an Indigenous American perspective, people are ‘Indigenous’ because they have family and clan-based ties to the community. When those ties don’t exist, stories fill the gap. But what if those stories are unverifiable? Or what if people take on ‘identities’ based on ‘knowledge’ that turns out not to be true, what then? How do they benefit from those narratives, whether true or not? Self-indigenisation based on self-identification describes people who claim to ‘be’ Indigenous, even when there is ample evidence that they have no Indigenous ancestry or lived experience as Indigenous people. It is a growing phenomenon in the United States and Canada as well as in other countries. Explaining why people pretend to be Indigenous when they aren’t is complicated, especially in light of the fact that the United Nations accepts self-identification as one criterion for indigeneity. However, in places where self-indigenisation has become egregious, it usually comes down to the fact that they perceive benefits, both material and psychological. The way it plays out varies from place to place, but there are commonalities across difference.

I am an Indigenous studies scholar in the US, and I study and wrote a book about self-indigenisation. I am an American Indian person, someone who comes from a long line of people who have been colonised. So mine is in part an insider perspective. As Native people, our experiences and cultures are unambiguous to us, if not always well known to others. They are well recorded in our families’ oral histories and usually in mountains of documentation, given that Indians are arguably the most documented ethnic group in the history of the US. Beginning with the earliest European settlers, missionaries and colonists kept track of the lives of Indigenous people for reasons including religious conversion, treaty negotiations, and census enumeration.

Anthropologists also, of course, study Indigenous people. The kinds of knowledge produced from external perspectives can vary widely from that which Indigenous people produce about themselves. Sometimes they conflict, but on occasion anthropologists’ research has helped tribes to recover lost knowledge. Both have their place. Anthropologists who study Indigenous cultural identity use the term ethnogenesis to describe how the identities of ethnic communities are formed or understood, and how they can change over time. Even Indigenous studies researchers recognise that, contrary to popular thought, Indigenous communities don’t remain static and unchanged over vast expanses of time. A popular tendency to misconceive of Indigenous people as gripped in terms of ‘authentic cultures’ doesn’t account for historical processes, including colonisation. History has imposed seismic changes on all Indigenous peoples, especially those who were in the way of foreign invasion and conquest. Expectations of cultural authenticity, then, can be a trap that doesn’t allow for peoples to experience history, to change with changing times.

In our modern world, there are of course many ways that cultures have evolved, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous. This blending of cultures through intermarriage has resulted in a blurring of lines that has made it difficult to make distinctions based on social constructions of race and ethnicity. Around the world, the questions are about what Indigeneity is and who decides, and how those questions are answered will vary. Laws and custom vary by country, and people will also make their own determinations. That said, there is also the very real phenomenon of ethnic fraud, the wrongful claiming of Indigeneity by people without any demonstrable connection to a historical Indigenous community. In extreme examples, these claims are based on flagrant lying.

Some anthropologists have identified a phenomenon they refer to as neo-Indianism. It was first named by Jacques Galinier and Antoinette Molinié, whose book The Neo-Indians: A Religion for the Third Millennium (translated from French by Lucy Lyall Grant, 2013) examined the rise of a new kind of Indigenism in Latin America where New Age rituals were invented for tourist consumption at Teotihuacan in Mexico, Cuzco in Peru, and other archaeological sites. Misrepresented as traditional Indigenous religion, the general public was unaware of the ruse even as it became a global industry. Similarly, there are growing instances of fake Aboriginal individuals in Australia. The same is happening in Aotearoa (New Zealand) among the Māori. Nowhere, however, is the problem of ethnic fraud more prevalent than in the US and Canada, where it is called ‘pretendianism’.

The Boy Scouts of America blatantly relied on playing Indian to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people

Pretendianism is sometimes known by the more benign-sounding term cultural appropriation, which describes an array of offensive behaviours, such as sports mascots or events with inappropriate names and imagery, Halloween costumes, or the flagrant, unauthorised use of Native spirituality and culture, such as pipe ceremonies and sweat lodges, just to name a few. In Germany, for example, there is an entire subculture dedicated to the fetishisation of Native Americans, which perpetuates harmful, inaccurate stereotypes. If we understand Nativeness conceptualised as a spectrum, then cultural appropriation, ethnic fraud and pretendianism can be understood as existing on the extreme end, at which claims to Indigeneity are objectively illegitimate.

The noted American Indian studies scholar Philip J Deloria coined the term ‘playing Indian’ with his seminal 1998 book of the same name, in which he traced a history of Americans’ penchant for adopting the dress and cultures of Native Americans for a variety of reasons, ranging from frivolous to serious and even politically motivated. The Boy Scouts of America, an extremely popular hobbyist club for children that romanticised America’s frontier days, blatantly relied on playing Indian in the early 20th century to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people. More than a century earlier, the 1773 Boston Tea Party, in which colonists costumed in Indian garb, was clearly a political incident that contributed to the incitement of a revolution. Many, many examples can be given of how the cultures of Native Americans are claimed for reasons that most Native people find offensive.

Pretendianism takes cultural appropriation to the next level when it goes beyond playing Indian to becoming Indian. People ‘become’ Indian when they claim to ‘be’ Indian with no connection to a tribal community, or little to no evidence of Native ancestry. It often begins with an individual who at some point in life transforms their identity claims from white (but sometimes other races or ethnicities) into Native American, based on family folklore or nothing at all, hence ‘race-shifting’, the term used in Australia. When those people have children and raise them with that mythology, pretendianism becomes generational. Amid many legitimate tribes who wrongfully lack political recognition by the US federal government, there are also hundreds of fake tribes that sprouted up in the 20th century. The majority of them claim to be Cherokee, but there are numerous others claiming to be Chumash, Shawnee, and more.

The work of Darryl Leroux shows how in Canada pretendianism is most prevalent in the east with a proliferation of ‘Abenaki’ groups. Faux Abenakis are also a problem in the state of Vermont, with four groups whom the state politically recognises but who have virtually no documentation to back up their claims of Abenaki descent. There are also dubious Metis and Inuit groups in Canada.

Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry

There are many pretendians whose names or faces you may recognise, emerging predominantly from the film industry. Perhaps most familiar is Iron Eyes Cody, who became best known as the ‘Crying Indian’ in the 1971 anti-littering commercial. Cody was not just an American actor who played Native American characters, he was an imposter of the highest order with a detailed but wildly false story about being Cherokee and Cree, which he wrote about in a 1980 autobiography. In 1996, a New Orleans Times-Picayune article revealed his true identity as the son of Italian immigrants. Born Espera Oscar de Corti, his film career began in the 1920s and spanned eight decades, with more than 200 film credits.

In Canada, the early 20th-century ‘Apache’ conservationist Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry. Both Belaney and Cody married Native women, which doubtless helped legitimise their false claims. The same was true for James Young Deer, a silent-film actor, director and producer who rose to fame working for the Pathé Frères film company. Young Deer falsely claimed to be Winnebago/Ho-Chunk, and married the actual Ho-Chunk actress Lilian St Cyr.

1 of 3

More recent exposures include Sacheen Littlefeather and Buffy Sainte-Marie. Littlefeather is best known as the ‘Native American’ woman who rejected an Oscar on behalf of Marlon Brando at the 1973 Academy Awards, ironically in the name of accurate representation of Native people in the film industry. I knew her for a decade before she died in 2022, and I document this story in detail in my book. A year after Littlefeather’s death, a bombshell story broke in the Canadian media that the rock-and-roll legend Buffy Sainte-Marie – who had risen to fame for her fiery Indian activism upon which her music was based – had fabricated a story about being born to a Piapot Cree family, adopted out, and raised by a white family. The evidence was overwhelmingly convincing that none of it was true.

There are many other examples of high-profile people who long claimed Native identities but with thin or non-existent evidence. In Canada, they include the celebrated author Joseph Boyden, the influential children’s rights lawyer Mary Ellen Turpel-LaFond, the prominent academic Carrie Bourassa, and the filmmaker Michelle Latimer, to name a few. In some of these cases, awards and honorary doctorates have been rescinded after investigations revealed their façades. In the US, one example stands out for the attention it received in the political arena. In a dramatic misstep, the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren in 2018 released the results of a DNA test in response to a challenge by the president Donald Trump about her claims to being Cherokee. The test showed that there was ‘strong evidence’ that she had a Native American ancestor six to 10 generations in the past. The Cherokee Nation, however, responded as it had for many years about her claims, that it had no record of Warren’s kinship to them, and that DNA does not always translate to Native identity or tribal belonging.

Pretendianism tends to be concentrated in entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, environmentalism and, increasingly, social media. In the US, the high-profile academics Ward Churchill and Andrea Smith, who lost their tenured professorships, have sparked intense debates about what it means to claim Native American identities with little or no evidence of connection to a tribal heritage. In another high-profile case, the University of California Berkeley professor Elizabeth Hoover drew the ire of Native American scholars after confessing that she had been wrongly claiming to be Mohawk throughout her career.

It’s safe to say that, in the US and Canada, no other non-white ethnicity is as commonly falsely claimed as the Indigenous identity. Explaining why is not as simple, however, and researchers continue to offer compelling and sometimes provocative answers. There is no single explanation, and even in the cases of Canada and the US, both former British colonies and neighbouring North American countries, there are different factors and nuances. And there is likely more than one point of origin, historically and geographically, which would mean a potential variety of reasons for why people ‘became’ Indian at certain moments in time.

That said, there is an explanation that fits within the long history of the US’s colonialism and American Indian policy. This perspective can help us understand the motivations of those who fraudulently become ‘Indian’ and the social landscape of various eras. It shows us that, for example, pretendianism is not just a matter of personal and individual pathology – it’s systemic, which explains why it is continually perpetuated.

One point of pretendianism’s origin is in the late 19th century, when the US, under the ideology of manifest destiny, was engaged in the violent dispossession of Native Americans. With the 1887 passage of the General Allotment Act came the brutality of boarding schools, family separation, forced religious conversion, and the allotment of Native lands. The boarding schools were tools of forced assimilation. Land allotment accomplished these objectives by confining Native Americans to reservations, and encouraging a sedentary life of farming and industry.

Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it

All aspects of assimilation meant to move Native Americans into a cash-based capitalist economy. Boarding schools and land allotment forced a shift in their fundamental way of life, one in which everything is commodified, a concept previously unknown in Native life.

By the 1920s, federal policymakers had recognised that assimilation was a catastrophic failure because it produced widespread poverty and all manner of social ills in reservation communities. Farming and ranching often proved to be unviable on many reservations. But there was one way that Native people could earn a lucrative living in the late 19th century: performing in the Wild West shows that were sweeping the country. The majority of Native Americans who were recruited to Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West show and others were veterans of the Plains Indian wars. For decades, the US had been fighting wars of aggression against Plains and other tribes in the west to force them on to reservations, thus freeing up vast tracts of land for settlers. Militarily defeated and succumbing to the US’s policy of Americanisation, many Indians went from prisoner-of-war camps to the Wild West shows. For the first time, Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it. This is the historical moment when Nativeness became a commodity, a way to make money from who one was, ethnically.

The US film industry has deep roots in the Wild West shows. Westerns were a prominent thematic genre of the early films, at a time when the US was contemplating the closing of the frontier. No longer a military threat, Native peoples became highly romanticised as Americans lamented the ‘vanishing Red Man’ in film. It was a natural progression, then, when the Show Indians became Movie Indians. It wasn’t long before people of other races and ethnicities began passing themselves off as Native Americans to obtain roles. The War Paint Club was the first Native American advocacy group, formed in 1926 to combat problems like fair representation and Native American roles for Native Americans in the industry.

In this way, Southern California became ground zero for the normalisation of Native ethnic fraud. Throughout the 20th century, other circumstances arose expanding opportunities to falsely claim Native American heritage based on no more than a family rumour, or simply the desire to profit financially. They included loose land-claims processes; changes in census rules that allowed for self-identification, and the reduction of the negative stigma of being Native American. In addition, a US government federal relocation programme in the 1950s led to urban Native American population centres where people with false claims could blend in as Native without community accountability; and a budding New Age industry that capitalised on all things Native American. California was the centre for all of these.

People are often mystified when they learn about the pretendian phenomenon; why would someone want to claim a heritage they weren’t born into? Identity commodification, coincident with the growth of Hollywood, gives us a conceptual tool to understand its historical particularity. Over the previous century, the opportunities for material gain associated with this ethnic fraud have only grown, and they show up in several specific spheres: film and entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, and environmental activism.

It’s not difficult to see why film and entertainment would attract opportunists looking to capitalise on an ethnically ambiguous appearance, paired with a convincing story. Iron Eyes Cody and Buffy Sainte-Marie were of Italian ancestry, and performativity is a key aspect of pretendianism. The ability to pass as Native American can be a door-opener, especially in casting rooms, but in other spaces as well. Yet, even when one does not ‘look’ stereotypically Native, a good story can compensate.

Fraudulently obtaining government contracts not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion

Stories help how many academics and authors deliver a compelling performance, regardless of whether they can pass as Native based on looks. In higher education, the ability to use words convincingly gives a leg up in competitive job markets, sometimes at the expense of actual, verifiably Native people. In academia, there is always caution about violating anti-discrimination laws, so hiring committees steer clear of asking about a person’s Native heritage, even when entire careers are built on identity claims. Such was the case with Elizabeth Hoover, whose environmental research in Mohawk communities was facilitated by her supposed Mohawk heritage.

In the publishing world, a gifted storyteller can cash in on the experiences of Native people. There are many books on the market by authors who co-opt Native culture, Native aesthetics, even Native trauma as though they are their own. In Canada, Boyden won many top Canadian book awards, honorary degrees and prestigious teaching appointments for his novels and short stories about Native life, based on his supposed lived experience. But Boyden was another fraudster, not a First Nations person, and is one of many examples of people who absorbed valuable resources meant for legitimate Indigenous people. Thanks to deep investigative journalism, his lack of Indigenous heritage was exposed in 2016. Boyden has since unconvincingly defended himself as having a small amount of Indigenous ancestry.

Native identity fraud also occurs in government contracting. In 2019, the Los Angeles Times conducted an investigation revealing that, since 2000, more than $300 million had gone to 12 companies claiming membership in three fake Cherokee tribes under federal, state and municipal programmes for minority businesses. One of the businesses turned out to be owned by the brother-in-law of the then-Congressional representative for California, Kevin McCarthy. Fraudulently obtaining government contracts does a double harm. It not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion toward legitimate tribally affiliated businesses.

Since the rise of the environmental movement in the 1970s, there has been a marked surge in Native American cultural appropriation, including patterns of Native becoming. During the US presidency of Joe Biden, we saw an elevation in influence of Indigenous cultural knowledge related to climate change resilience strategies up to the highest levels of policymaking, including the White House. The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the Inflation Reduction Act and other legislation that privileged green energy, environmental justice and Indigenous knowledge in climate resilience projects brought material benefits to Native communities through unprecedented levels of funding for environmental and energy projects. But fraud dilutes its effectiveness.

The surge in funding coincided with a proliferation of Indigenous conservation and environmental nonprofit organisations. In many cases, Indigenous conservation groups were led by legitimately Indigenous people. But when grant programmes are opened up to groups who are not federally recognised tribes, there tends to be far less scrutiny about who the leaders are of an ‘Indigenous led’ group. The same is true in the philanthropy world. Private funders are often ill-equipped to make those kinds of determinations and sometimes fear that enquiring about them is rude or even illegal. Too often, the result has been the distribution of grants (in the environmental sector and beyond) to people or groups posing as Native, but with no verifiable Native American heritage.

There are other ways that posing as an Native American can be lucrative. Again in California, for example, where there is a proliferation of groups that call themselves ‘tribes’. Some are more legit than others, and there is no law prohibiting a group from calling itself a tribe. One group known as the Northern Chumash Tribal Council (NCTC) near San Luis Obispo, for instance, began as a ‘cultural monitoring’ group, overseeing the development of sensitive sites where there might be Native American human remains or other burial items. Contracts for cultural monitoring can command hundreds of thousands of dollars and, while laws allow only the ‘most likely descendants’ to monitor a site, they are notoriously lax. Fred Harvey Collins, the founder of NCTC, also went on to lead an effort to establish a national marine sanctuary, garnering significant attention and massive cultural and financial support. However, a legal battle involving his ancestry revealed in 2017 that he possessed no Native American heritage.

Claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past

Not everyone who dubiously calls themselves Native American does it for financial gain. In the US and Canada, it is wildly common to hear people talk about having ‘Indian blood’ or a mysterious Native American ancestor somewhere in the family tree, with no evidence whatsoever to back up the family lore. Sometimes, commercial DNA tests will suggest trace amounts of Indigenous ancestry in the distant past (recall Warren’s case), but as the scholar Kim TallBear has shown in Native American DNA (2012), from a Native standpoint, without a tribal community or family ties, DNA isn’t enough to legitimately call oneself Native American, and certainly not with any legal standing.

So what’s in it for them – what are the benefits of untruthfully claiming Native American heritage?

There are psychological, affective benefits to thinking one has a linkage, however distant, to the ‘original Americans’. Who, after all, is more ‘American’ than Native Americans? In another strand of reasoning, claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past. If one is the colonised, they must not be coloniser. Self-indigenising is a way to be absolved of responsibility for the crimes of colonialism and maintain the fiction of familial innocence.

Ultimately, though, in a country founded on the rights to private property and free speech, identity is perceived as a personal possession, something one can claim at will. In the US, there is a strong common belief that a person can be whoever and whatever they say they are, regardless of facts or evidence.

Native people have come to see the stakes of pretendianism as higher than ever. When university and entertainment jobs, contracts and grants meant for actual Native Americans are taken by people with no connection to legitimate tribal communities, it constitutes stealing resources from the descendants of people who have already been victimised by centuries of theft and loss. Money that is meant to help mitigate those patterns of erasure is unintentionally rendered a tool of more erasure.

At the same time, determining who is Native is not always a simple or easy task. There is a wide, grey area on the spectrum of Nativeness, where people can be legitimately Native American and not be an enrolled member of a federally recognised tribe. Confusion and fear about how to determine who is legitimately Native in our institutions has contributed to the perpetuation of pretendianism. There is growing recognition that something can and must be done to ensure that the resources meant for Native people go to Native people.

In the US, this has long been acknowledged in the art world. Since 1935, the Native American art market has been governed by the Indian Arts and Crafts Board, a US government agency within the Department of the Interior. It was originally set up to encourage the growth of the market, promoting economic self-sufficiency of ‘federally recognised American Indians and Alaska Natives (Indians)’. In 1990, US Congress passed the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, a truth-in-advertising law with strict requirements that anyone selling art as ‘Indian’-made should be enrolled in a federal or state-recognised tribe, or be a certified artisan of the tribe. It is meant to ensure authenticity, in turn guarding the commercial value of Indian-made art. While the law is widely viewed as deeply flawed for the ways it excludes documented Native people and simultaneously includes people from state-recognised groups, it does act as a bulwark against fraud.

Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when leveraged for financial or professional gain

The art world is virtually the only realm of social life with regulatory guardrails against Native ethnic fraud. Aside from this, those addressing the issue with the most urgency are in universities, particularly in Canada. There, a few colleges have implemented verification processes for admissions and scholarship applications. In the US, fears about violating race-based anti-discrimination laws present significant obstacles to implementing similar verification procedures.

Scholars push back against these fears by emphasising that Native Americans are more accurately understood as a political group than as a racial group by virtue of their sovereignty. Verification involves questions about relationships to claimed tribal communities, not questions about race. It’s not unlike asking for proof of military service for those who seek a veteran’s benefits. Wrongly claiming to be a veteran is called stolen valour and can lead to legal consequences. Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when it is leveraged for financial or professional gain. At the very least, it should not be rewarded.

The pretendian wars that Indigenous people are fighting in the US and abroad are aimed at spreading awareness that wrongful Native-claiming is not a harmless frivolity. Valuable resources are being diverted from those to whom they are intended. In some cases, it is a criminal offence, and more needs to be done to guard against it. It should be just as socially unacceptable to illicitly claim Native American heritage as it is to illicitly claim to be a military veteran. People with unsubstantiated stories about Native American heritage should seriously rethink those claims before perpetuating them. They should do the research to find out the truth, but if no evidence is found, they should stop repeating the story. They should also remember that DNA tests showing Indigenous ancestry do not substitute for kinship; this is how belonging is determined in most tribal communities. Until then, Native people are sounding the alarm bells with urgency and determination.
